outputs.L1:
All the hills and vales along,  
Earth is bursting into song,  
And the singers are the chaps  
Who are going to die, perhaps.

O sing, marching men,  
Till the valleys ring again.  
Give your gladness to Earth’s keeping;  
So be glad when you are sleeping.

Cast away regret and rue;  
Think what you are marching to.  
Little live, great pass.  
Jesus Christ and Barabbas  
Were found the same day:  
This died; that went his way.

So sing with joyful breath,  
For, why, you are going to death.  
Teeming Earth will surely store  
All the gladness that you pour.

Earth that never doubts nor fears,  
Earth that knows of death, not tears,  
Earth that bore with joyful ease  
Hemlock for Socrates,  
Earth that blossomed and was glad  
’Neath the cross that Christ had,  
Shall rejoice and blossom too  
When the bullet reaches you.

Wherefore, men marching  
On the road to death, sing!  
Pour your gladness on Earth’s head;  
So be merry, so be dead.

From the hills and valleys, Earth  
Shouts back the sound of mirth:  
Tramp of feet and lilt of song  
Ringing all the road along.

All the music of their going—  
Ringing, swinging, glad song-throwing—  
Earth will echo still, when foot  
Lies numb and voice mute.

On, marching men, on  
To the gates of death with song.  
Sow your gladness for Earth’s reaping,  
So you may be glad, though sleeping.

Strew your gladness on Earth’s bed;  
So be merry, so be dead.
outputs.L2:
Across every ridge and hollow,  
The whole world swells with music,  
Raised by young men who may soon  
Meet their deaths.  
Keep singing, soldiers on the march,  
Until the lowlands answer.  
Entrust your happiness to the soil,  
And remain joyful even in final sleep.  

Abandon sorrow and remorse;  
Remember the end toward which you advance.  
The insignificant endure; the mighty depart.  
Jesus Christ and Barabbas  
Faced judgment upon one day:  
One was killed, while the other walked free.  
Therefore, fill your voices with delight,  
Since death is your destination.  
The abundant earth will preserve  
Every measure of joy you spill upon it.  

The ground neither hesitates nor trembles;  
It understands dying, but not weeping.  
Gladly and without complaint,  
It produced the hemlock that killed Socrates.  
It flowered in happiness  
Below the cross borne by Christ.  
Likewise, it will celebrate and bloom  
When a bullet strikes you.  
Thus, you soldiers traveling  
Along the path toward death—sing!  
Crown the world with your cheerfulness:  
Be joyful, and then be dead.  

From mountain and dale, the earth  
Returns their cries of celebration.  
The pounding rhythm of boots and buoyant melody  
Resound throughout the length of the road.  
Every note accompanying their departure—  
Pealing, swaying, casting happiness abroad—  
Will continue to reverberate through the world  
After feet are motionless and voices silent.  

Forward, marching soldiers, forward;  
Approach death’s entrance singing.  
Plant your happiness for the earth to harvest,  
That joy may remain yours in sleep.  
Scatter your delight over the world’s resting place:  
Be merry, and be dead.
outputs.L3:
The poem urges marching soldiers to sing joyfully, even though they may be advancing toward their deaths. Rather than dwelling on fear or regret, the men are encouraged to cast aside sorrow and offer their happiness freely to the earth. This emphasis on joy in the face of mortality gives their march both courage and dignity.

References to Christ, Barabbas, and Socrates place the soldiers’ fate within a much broader history of sacrifice, condemnation, and death. These figures suggest that mortality is universal and that the soldiers belong to a long tradition of people who have faced death, whether unjustly, willingly, or inevitably.

At the same time, the earth is portrayed as enduring death without grief. It receives the dead and transforms the gladness they leave behind into new life, growth, and blossoming. Although the soldiers’ feet will eventually stop marching and their voices will fall silent, their joy will not disappear. Their songs will continue to resonate symbolically through the earth, preserved in the life that emerges after them.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts the grim reality of soldiers marching toward almost certain death, yet it refuses to surrender to despair. Instead, the soldiers are urged to sing as they advance, meeting mortality with courage, fellowship, and joy. Their song becomes an act of defiance: although war may destroy their bodies and silence their individual voices, it cannot erase the vitality they express in their final moments. By pouring their strength and gladness into the earth, they become part of something larger and more enduring than themselves.

Nature thus serves as both witness and memorial. The earth receives the fallen soldiers, while the surrounding landscape preserves the emotional force of their song. Their joy seems to pass into the fields, trees, wind, and future seasons, continuing after they are gone. In this way, death is not presented simply as an ending. The soldiers’ physical lives may be brief, but their courage and affirmation of life endure through the natural world. The poem therefore transforms a march toward death into a powerful celebration of human resilience, suggesting that even in the face of destruction, joy can leave a lasting echo.
outputs.L5:
**All, And, Till**

All we carry are memories, hopes, and the courage to continue. We walk together through changing seasons, sharing laughter and silence, victories and mistakes. Till the road ends—or a new one begins—we keep moving forward, believing that every ending holds the promise of another beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the full text of Charles Hamilton Sorley’s poem “All the Hills and Vales Along.”
counterfactuals.output:
## “All the Hills and Vales Along”  
*Charles Hamilton Sorley*

All the hills and vales along  
Earth is bursting into song,  
And the singers are the chaps  
Who are going to die perhaps.

O sing, marching men,  
Till the valleys ring again.  
Give your gladness to earth’s keeping,  
So be glad, when you are sleeping.

Cast away regret and rue,  
Think what you are marching to.  
Little live, great pass.  
Jesus Christ and Barabbas  
Were found the same day.  
This died hard, and that died well.  
And both went to Hell.  
Who shall judge? Who shall tell?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
